summary:
New Jersey's Law Against Discrimination, amended in 2006 to cover gender identity and expression and in 1991 to cover affectional or sexual orientation, bars denial of goods, services, facilities and lodging on those grounds in places of public accommodation, which state materials describe as including hotels, restaurants, stores and transportation, as well as in housing and employment. A trans visitor refused service or lodging can complain to the Division on Civil Rights, which investigates and can grant relief.

Bias-motivated crimes carry enhanced penalties where the bias rests on gender identity or expression, with sensitivity training available as a sentencing condition. A bill extending bias and intimidation protections to gender identity passed the lower house 71-0 in March 2021. The FBI's New Jersey division has reported gender X in its data since June 2021, a July 2022 police licensing system carries gender-identity protections, and state-run hospital patient records are required to protect sexual orientation and gender identity data.

State identity documents are comparatively open. Since 1 February 2019 a transgender person may obtain an amended birth certificate with corrected name and sex without surgery or any medical procedure, under three laws signed in June 2018; those laws also created an X marker on official documents and put transgender and intersex people on death certificates. Since February 2020 no doctor's note is required to change the M or F marker on a driver licence or state ID, and since April 2021 the X, M and F markers are all available. A November 2022 executive order provides privacy and confidentiality in legal name changes. These are state documents; passport and visa issuance is governed separately by federal rules.

An April 2023 executive order directs state agencies to protect and defend gender-affirming healthcare within New Jersey's borders, including access by people travelling in from other states.

The state has recognised and performed marriages of same-sex couples since 21 October 2013, following a 27 September 2013 court decision whose appeal was rejected on 19 October 2013; the legislature codified the position in December 2021 and the governor signed it on 10 January 2022, effective immediately. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status can marry and have that marriage recognised here.

A January 2020 law bars the gay and transgender panic defence, providing that provocation is not objectively reasonable when based on actual or perceived gender identity or expression, including an unwanted non-forcible romantic or sexual advance. The bill passed both chambers 73-0 and 39-0.

A July 2026 legal-risk ranking built from a rubric over thousands of tracked anti-trans bills places New Jersey in the fifteen-state Most Protective tier, alongside California, Colorado, Connecticut, Hawaii, Illinois, Massachusetts, Maryland, Minnesota, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont and Washington.
tangentialFactors:
The same ranking places the worst-scoring states at the opposite end, with penalties of up to five years' imprisonment in Idaho and an arrest policy for gender-identity bathroom use in Florida. A trans visitor crossing out of New Jersey enters a materially different enforcement environment.

New Jersey's sodomy statute was struck down in 1978 in State v. Ciuffini as a violation of privacy and autonomy, and the legislature repealed it the same year. In 1967 One Eleven Liquors, Inc. v. Division of Alcoholic Beverage Commission invalidated licence revocations applied to venues serving female impersonators or persons of ill repute; the attorney general issued an official apology in June 2021.

Sex while infected with any sexually transmitted infection, including HIV, was reduced from a third-degree offence for HIV and a fourth-degree offence for other infections to a disorderly persons offence by S3707, signed 18 January 2022.
localsOnly:
The three June 2018 laws, including the Babs Siperstein Law, removed the proof-of-surgery requirement for birth-certificate changes, made New Jersey the seventeenth state to allow surgery-free changes and the fourth with a third birth-certificate option after California, Oregon and Washington, and established a Transgender Task Force of government officials, legal, policy and medical experts and community advocates.

September 2018 state school guidance promotes policies on names and pronouns, participation in activities, use of facilities and student records, and the New Jersey State Interscholastic Athletic Association allows participation according to gender identity. In June 2023 school boards in Middletown, Marlboro and Manalapan-Englishtown adopted parental-notification policies that out transgender and non-binary students; the attorney general's office sued to block them, describing the policies as potentially violating discrimination and hate-crime legislation.

Sexual orientation change efforts directed at minors were banned by legislation passed in June 2013 and signed 19 August 2013, upheld in District Court on 8 November 2013 and in the Third Circuit on 11 September 2014, with Supreme Court review declined in May 2015 and again on 15 April 2019 in King v. Murphy. A Hudson County ruling held that claiming to cure a disorder is fraud.
outOfScopeNotes:
The July 2026 tier placement is an advocacy rubric over tracked bill counts rather than a measure of enforcement on the ground; no complaint or prosecution statistics for the Law Against Discrimination's gender-identity provisions were located in the sources.

The outcome of the attorney general's suit against the three school boards is not sourced, and whether those parental-notification policies remain in force is unresolved.

The April 2023 executive order's effect on out-of-state subpoenas or warrants seeking patient records from New Jersey providers is not described in the sources.

Whether the state bias-crime enhancements have been applied in any prosecution involving a transgender victim is not documented in the sources.
